failures.title: BMW B58D30M1 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Cooling System Leaks - water pump and coolant loss
items.whatHappens: The B58's water pump is a known weak point, with the shaft seal failing and coolant leaking from the weep hole at the bottom of the pump. Owners report sudden low‑coolant warnings, coolant pooling under the vehicle, and in some cases the water pump pulley disintegrating, throwing the auxiliary belt. The B58's sophisticated dual‑circuit cooling system can also suffer from premature coolant breakdown and gassing, leading to pressure loss.
items.repairVsReplace: Water pump replacement alone typically resolves the issue and costs £500-£1,000 at an independent specialist. If ignored, overheating can cause head gasket failure or cylinder head damage - at which point a full engine replacement becomes the more economical route. → Read our full cooling system failure guide

items.title: Oil Pump Failure - plastic internal components (2019-2022 models)
items.whatHappens: B58 engines produced between 2019 and 2022 were fitted with oil pumps containing plastic internal components, particularly a plastic outer ring in the variable‑pressure design. These plastic parts can crack - especially in cold conditions - leading to sudden oil pressure loss and catastrophic engine failure. BMW quietly switched to an all‑metal oil pump design from 2020 onward.
items.repairVsReplace: The oil pump itself can be replaced proactively (£800-£1,500 parts and labour), but if the pump fails while driving, the engine is typically destroyed - full replacement is the only option. → Read our full oil pump failure guide

items.title: High‑Pressure Fuel Pump (HPFP) Failure
items.whatHappens: The B58's direct‑injection high‑pressure fuel pump can fail due to manufacturing defects or contaminated fuel. Symptoms include engine misfires, loss of power under acceleration, difficulty starting, and rough idling. The HPFP is a common replacement item on higher‑mileage B58 units.
items.repairVsReplace: HPFP replacement (£800-£1,500) is straightforward and usually resolves the issue. If left unaddressed, fuel starvation can cause lean running and eventual engine damage.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the B58D30M1
variants.intro: The B58D30M1 (also designated B58B30M1) is the Technical Update (TU) version of BMW's B58 engine, introduced from 2019 onward. It sits within the broader B58 family and is commonly confused with: | Similar Code | What It Is | Link | |---|---|---| | B58B30M0 | First‑generation B58 (2015-2019) - fitted to F30 340i, F32 440i, G11 740i, early G01 X3 M40i | BMW B58B30M0 engine | | B58B30O1 | Higher‑output B58 TU variant - 374 hp, fitted to later M340i, Z4 M40i, Supra | BMW B58B30O1 engine | | B58B30C | Mild‑hybrid B58 variant - fitted to 540i, X5 xDrive40i, X7 xDrive40i | BMW B58B30C engine | How to find your engine code: The engine code is stamped on a metal plate on the cylinder block, visible from the driver's side of the engine bay, and also appears on the V5C registration document and in the vehicle's VIN (digits 4-7). If you're unsure, enter your registration above - we'll confirm your exact fitment. Why the difference matters: The B58D30M1 (TU) benefits from a revised timing chain tensioner design, improved PCV system, and - on post‑2020 units - an all‑metal oil pump. Fitting an earlier B58B30M0 (non‑TU) into a TU‑spec vehicle is not a straight swap; the ECU calibration, cooling system plumbing, and turbocharger mounting differ.

relatives.description: - the first‑generation B58 (2015-2019) fitted to F30 340i, F32 440i, G11 740i and early G01 X3 M40i; it lacks the TU’s revised timing chain tensioner and improved PCV system, and is more prone to VANOS solenoid issues.
- the 374 hp high‑output TU variant found in later M340i, Z4 M40i and Toyota Supra; it uses a different turbocharger and calibration, making it not a direct swap into B58D30M1‑spec vehicles.

- a lower‑output (333 hp) TU variant fitted to some 540i, X5 and X7 models; it shares the same block and most hardware but runs a different ECU map. If your car is a 540i, check which code you have before ordering.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement B58D30M1 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used B58D30M1 can make sense for lower‑value hosts (e.g. higher‑mileage G20 M340i or G30 540i) where a reconditioned unit would exceed the vehicle's value. However, used units carry significant risk: you don't know the oil pump generation (pre‑2020 plastic vs post‑2020 metal), the cooling system history, or whether the HPFP is on its way out. Only consider a used unit with documented service history and a compression test.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: For most B58D30M1 replacements, a professionally reconditioned unit is the right call. A proper recon addresses the engine's known weak points: the water pump and thermostat are replaced, the HPFP is inspected or replaced, the oil pump is upgraded to the all‑metal design (if the core is pre‑2020), and all gaskets and seals are renewed. With a 12-24 month warranty, this is the lowest‑risk option for a £3,800-£6,000 supply‑only investment.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for this engine only when the original block is in good condition and the vehicle has significant sentimental or collector value - e.g. a low‑mileage Z4 M40i or a well‑specified 8 Series. A performance‑oriented rebuild can include upgraded forged internals, but for most owners, a reconditioned exchange unit offers better value.
